1a5e95ea29520134aa86161df09979c2e217d020.summary: A 2017 blog post by Brian Reitz that builds a PowerShell proof of concept, using the PSReflect tool, to write a Windows registry Run key value whose name starts with a null character. The post links this persistence trick to Kovter malware. It says Regedit and similar tools fail to show the value, while the Sysinternals Autoruns tool still does. The author presents it to help defenders test detection of such registry persistence.

1acc2a8d239c6e3174bbec8dcce33dc1175d6f02.summary: This page is a promotional landing page for a Qualys Threat Research Team report on Quasar RAT, an open-source remote access trojan. It invites readers to download the full report without registration. The page gives only a short overview and asks readers to download the rest, so it is treated as a marketing piece and the fact lists are left empty.

1aa5a21d68cedb2cffb923a011be8e5cd7b1bb64.summary: eSentire's Threat Response Unit disrupted an intrusion at a product safety testing organization in late July, before any ransomware was deployed. The attackers gained access through a vulnerable SharePoint server and used a web shell, Cobalt Strike, Mimikatz and Metasploit. The intrusion was linked to the Hello Ransomware group, and its techniques resembled those of Chinese espionage groups such as Emissary Panda. The report stresses that attribution is uncertain and that the attack could be a false flag. It also discusses wider claims about China, Russia and ransomware.

hedges: The attack could be part of a false flag campaign.
TRU has no strong evidence connecting Chinese espionage groups and Hello Ransomware, only an overlap in techniques and tools.
Unit 42 notes similarities to Emissary Panda campaigns but hesitates to draw conclusions.
FireEye suggests the 2019 SharePoint campaigns are run by UNC215, which may or may not be directly associated with Emissary Panda.
The operators might be intentionally adopting known Chinese tactics to mislead attribution efforts.
It is impossible to tell which implementation of Mimikatz was used.
The potential Russian origins of the application used for the 2017 version are only potential, not established.
Possible scenarios include evolution of China's cybercrime economy, national interest in ransomware, or a non-Chinese group intentionally adopting Chinese tactics.
